What y ou hav e learnt
/square6Elements can be classified as metals and non-metals.
/square6Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and are good conductors of heat and
electricity. They are solids at room temperature, except mercury which is a liquid.
/square6Metals can form positive ions by losing electrons to non-metals.
/square6Metals combine with oxygen to form basic oxides. Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide
show the properties of both basic as well as acidic oxides. These oxides are known
as amphoteric oxides.
/square6Different metals have different reactivities with water and dilute acids.
/square6A list of common metals arranged in order of their decreasing reactivity is known
as an activity series.
/square6Metals above hydrogen in the Activity series can displace hydrogen from dilute
acids.
/square6A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
/square6Metals occur in nature as free elements or in the form of their compounds.
/square6The extraction of metals from their ores and then refining them for use is known
as metallurgy.
/square6An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a
non-metal.
/square6The surface of some metals, such as iron, is corroded when they are exposed to
moist air for a long period of time. This phenomenon is known as corrosion.
/square6Non-metals have properties opposite to that of metals. They are neither malleable
nor ductile. They are bad conductors of heat and electricity, except for graphite,
which conducts electricity.

Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides.

 For example, when copper is heated in air , it combines with oxygen
